title: AI-Driven Credit Risk Assessment in Fintech Lending: Implications for Financial Inclusion, Systemic Risk, and Regulatory Governance
venue: American International Journal of Business Management
tldr: Systematic review of 30 peer-reviewed articles reveals that ensemble and hybrid explainable AI models outperform traditional credit scoring but require integrated governance frameworks addressing fairness, systemic risk, and regulatory gaps.
problem_and_motivation: AI and ML models have transformed credit risk assessment in fintech lending, yet their adoption introduces three unresolved tensions: the accuracy-explainability trade-off, the inclusion-bias paradox, and the stability-innovation dilemma. Traditional credit scoring excludes over 80% of adults in emerging economies, while unregulated AI deployment may amplify systemic risk and inequality. No existing governance framework jointly addresses model-level performance, borrower fairness, and market-level systemic stability.
approach: Systematic literature review of 30 peer-reviewed articles published between 2012 and 2025, following a PRISMA-inspired screening protocol from 280 initial documents.
Comparative analysis of ML model performance (AUC-ROC, Gini, KS) across logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, XGBoost, LightGBM, LSTM, and hybrid XAI models.
Synthesis of financial inclusion metrics across regional fintech lending contexts including Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Latin America, EU, and North America.
Jurisdictional comparison of AI credit governance frameworks across the US, EU, UK, China, and emerging markets using SAFE AI pillar alignment.
Theoretical framework construction using information asymmetry theory, financial innovation theory, and systemic risk theory as complementary anchors.
Development of the Integrated AI Credit Risk Framework (IACRF) mapping four SAFE AI principles onto five operational lifecycle stages.
Formulation of four theoretical propositions connecting model performance, financial inclusion, systemic risk, and governance adoption outcomes.
Identification of three systemic risk propagation pathways specific to AI-driven lending: model herding, procyclicality, and platform contagion.
findings: num: Gradient boosting models achieve AUC-ROC of 0.83-0.91, which is 7-19 percentage points higher than logistic regression baselines.
num: Hybrid XAI model combining gradient boosting with SHAP achieves AUC-ROC of 0.89 versus 0.76 for logistic regression baseline.
num: LSTM networks achieve AUC-ROC above 0.90 but with very low interpretability and incompatibility with EU AI Act requirements.
num: AI credit models increase thin-file borrower approval rates by 20-40 percentage points in emerging market settings.
AI systems systematically encode historical discriminatory patterns from training data, and XAI techniques identify but cannot remediate bias alone.
Three systemic risk propagation pathways — model herding, procyclicality, and platform contagion — compound each other beyond traditional credit monocultures.
The IACRF operationalizes four SAFE AI pillars across five lifecycle stages from data governance to impact evaluation.
Regulatory governance is jurisdictionally fragmented, with the EU AI Act closest to best practice but lacking systemic risk monitoring tools.
Emerging markets face the highest governance gaps despite hosting populations most vulnerable to the inclusion-bias paradox.
key_figures_tables: Table 1: Comparative performance of AI/ML models in credit risk assessment → Ensemble and hybrid XAI models dominate AUC-ROC while balancing interpretability.
Figure 1: IACRF conceptual architecture with five lifecycle stages → Maps SAFE AI pillars to operational governance from data to impact evaluation.
Table 2: Financial inclusion metrics by region in AI-driven lending → Sub-Saharan Africa shows highest approval uplift but also highest digital exclusion risk.
Figure 2: PRISMA-informed literature search and screening flowchart → 280 initial documents narrowed to 30 peer-reviewed articles.
Table 3: Comparative AI credit governance frameworks by jurisdiction → Governance gaps range from 2/5 in EU and UK to 5/5 in emerging markets.
Figure 3: Systemic risk propagation pathways in AI-driven fintech lending → Three pathways compound each other to amplify systemic vulnerability.

definitions.definition: Artificial Intelligence — computational systems performing tasks requiring human-like reasoning and decision-making.
Machine Learning — subset of AI where algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions.
Explainable AI — methods such as SHAP and LIME that make machine learning model decisions interpretable.
Integrated AI Credit Risk Framework — five-stage governance framework operationalizing SAFE AI principles across the fintech credit lifecycle.
Governance framework with four pillars: Statistical accuracy, Algorithmic fairness, Financial stability, and Ethical governance.
Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve — metric measuring binary classification model performance.
SHapley Additive exPlanations — game-theoretic approach to explain individual machine learning predictions.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations — technique for explaining individual predictions of any classifier.
Fair Isaac Corporation — entity producing the dominant consumer credit scoring system used since 1989.
Peer-to-peer — lending model connecting borrowers directly with individual lenders through digital platforms.
Buy Now Pay Later — deferred payment option integrated into merchant checkout processes.
Equal Credit Opportunity Act — US federal law prohibiting discrimination in credit transactions.
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — US agency enforcing consumer financial protection laws.
Financial Stability Board — international body monitoring and making recommendations for the global financial system.
European Banking Authority — EU body ensuring effective and consistent prudential regulation of credit institutions.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a comprehensive systematic review synthesizing evidence on AI/ML model performance, financial inclusion impacts, algorithmic bias, and systemic risk in fintech credit assessment. It introduces the Integrated AI Credit Risk Framework (IACRF), a novel five-stage governance architecture operationalizing SAFE AI principles across the fintech credit lifecycle. The paper identifies three systemic risk propagation pathways — model herding, procyclicality, and platform contagion — specific to AI-driven lending that compound beyond traditional credit monocultures. It provides a jurisdictional comparison of regulatory frameworks revealing governance gaps between developed and emerging markets. The work bridges isolated research streams on model performance, inclusion, bias, and systemic risk into a unified analytical framework with four testable theoretical propositions.

topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All fourteen topic domains were systematically scanned for citeable claims. Domain 4 (Existing Systems) was flagged as relevant at low level: 4.A for surveying the fintech lending landscape and 4.B for identifying gaps in traditional credit scoring. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was flagged at medium level: 6.A for comparative ML model performance analysis. Domain 10 (Privacy and Trust) was flagged at medium level: 10.A for data governance and consent architecture discussion, and 10.B for algorithmic fairness and explainability analysis. Domain 12 (Evaluation) was flagged at medium level: 12.B for systematic model evaluation across metrics. Domains 1-3 (Filipino demographics, financial behavior, expense categorization) were considered and rejected as the paper does not address personal finance management or Filipino-specific contexts. Domains 5 (Behavioral Profiles), 7 (Budgeting), 8 (Anomaly Detection), 9 (Mobile Design), 11 (Engagement), 13 (Savings/Debt), and 14 (Synthetic Data/Deployment) were considered and rejected as the paper focuses on institutional credit risk rather than personal finance system design. Domain 5 was borderline for behavioral data discussion but rejected because the paper addresses credit scoring behavioral data, not personal spending behavioral profiles. The overall topical coverage centers on AI governance and credit risk, tangentially relevant to the PFMS domain through ML evaluation methodology and data privacy principles.

limitations: Relies on published literature only, restricting causal inference and evaluation of unpublished industry practices.
